flawed_step: To prove the claim you would need to show that every neighbour of a vertex with degree at least 2 cannot also have degree at least 2. Nothing in the definition of a tree forces this. The claim holds for n ≤ 4, but it fails at n = 5, where a central vertex can have only non-leaf neighbours.
counterexample: Take the path P5 with vertices 1-2-3-4-5 and edges {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,4}, {4,5}. It is a tree on n=5 vertices, and 2 <= 5 <= 7. The degrees are deg(1)=1, deg(2)=2, deg(3)=2, deg(4)=2 and deg(5)=1. Vertex 3 has degree 2, and its only neighbours are 2 and 4. Both of those have degree 2, so neither is a leaf. Vertex 3 is therefore not adjacent to any leaf. (P6 and P7 fail in the same way.)
assessment_summary: The claim is false. Any tree that is a path with at least 5 vertices is a counterexample. In P5, the middle vertex has degree 2, but its two neighbours also have degree 2, so it touches no leaf. For n ≤ 4 every tree does satisfy the property: at n=2 there is no vertex of degree 2 or more, at n=3 the only tree is a path whose centre touches both leaves, and at n=4 the path's inner vertices each touch a leaf and the star's centre does too. But the statement covers n up to 7, so it is invalid.
